abstract_sentences.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) is the method of choice for training models in setups where the objective function can only be evaluated by sampling from the model.
Our key observation is that when the feedback is terminal and binary, models implicitly induce a likelihood over correct rollouts.
abstract_sentences.transition_from_previous: narrows scope to terminal binary feedback

abstract_sentences.text: Maximum likelihood would be the natural framework in such settings, but RL is used instead as a workaround to the non-differentiability.
We prove that the standard, expected-reward RL formulation is only a first-order approximation of the likelihood.

To remedy this mismatch, we introduce Maximum Likelihood Reinforcement Learning (MaxRL), a compute-indexed family of sample-based objectives that interpolate between expected-reward RL and maximum likelihood as sampling compute is scaled.
The resulting objective is a one-line change to standard RL implementations.

MaxRL Pareto-dominates existing methods in all tested models and tasks, achieves up to 20× gains in test-time scaling efficiency over GRPO, and scales more favorably with additional training data and compute.

abstract_summary.reported_results: Claims Pareto dominance in all tested models/tasks and up to 20× test-time scaling efficiency over GRPO.

method_analysis.formal_objects: Input x~rho; correct output y*(x); output distribution p_theta; latent policy m_theta; deterministic decode f; binary reward; pass rate p; pass@k; truncation T; samples N; successes K; score S_i.
method_analysis.input_output_state_objective_assumptions: Input is x; output is a decoded y/f(z); state is a sampled latent trajectory; objective is expected log pass rate approximated by a finite harmonic pass@k sum; assumptions include terminal binary correctness and i.i.d. rollout sampling.

method_analysis.equation_count: 11 numbered equations in the main body (Eq. (1)–(11)); approximately 17 main-body display blocks by physical layout; appendix adds approximately 26 display blocks and proof derivations.
method_analysis.algorithm_detail: Algorithm 1 inputs batch B, rollout count N, and latent policy; it loops over inputs and rollouts, computes binary rewards and scores, forms mean reward and normalized advantages, averages gradients, and returns g. Its key invariant is zero gradient when the per-task mean reward is zero.
method_analysis.complexity_statement: No asymptotic computational-complexity theorem is stated; the operative compute axis is number of rollouts N/T.

claim_closure.claim: Expected-reward RL is a first-order approximation of the ML objective in binary correctness settings.
claim_closure.method_response: Defines pass rate and contrasts JML with JRL; derives Eq. (4)–(5).
claim_closure.evidence_response: Appendix C proves the conditional-gradient identity; ImageNet uses CE as the direct-ML comparison.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion re-establishes MaxRL as an ML framework for non-differentiable binary reward settings.

claim_closure.claim: A rollout-indexed family interpolates between RL and ML.
claim_closure.method_response: Eq. (6)–(7) define the T-truncated objective; Proposition 6 supplies its weight function.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 2 and Figure 13 test increased rollout counts in controlled and GSM8K settings.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion says MaxRL approaches maximum likelihood as compute increases.

claim_closure.claim: The successful-trajectory estimator exactly matches a finite MaxRL objective.
claim_closure.method_response: Theorem 2 states unbiasedness at T=N; Algorithm 1 is the practical estimator.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Appendix D proves the practical dropped-baseline estimator is T=N−1 instead.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion does not repeat the N−1 qualification.

claim_closure.claim: MaxRL Pareto-dominates existing methods in all tested settings.
claim_closure.method_response: Weight-function analysis motivates the distinction from RL and GRPO.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Reports ImageNet, maze, GSM8K, Qwen3, and broad appendix baselines, but no run-to-run uncertainty or exhaustive baseline space.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion repeats stronger scaling/advantages at the stated scope.

claim_closure.claim: Hard-prompt weighting causes improved coverage and avoids distribution sharpening.
claim_closure.origin: Section 5 mechanism and Section 6.5 behavior analysis.
claim_closure.method_response: w(p) predicts greater emphasis on low-pass-rate inputs.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figures 6, 7, 14, 27, and 29 are aligned behavioral observations, not an intervention that isolates this mechanism.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion does not state a causal proof of the mechanism.

claim_closure.claim: MaxRL creates capabilities beyond the base model.
claim_closure.method_response: No general theorem is supplied for this claim.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Table 10 and Figure 30 cover 30 AIME 2025 questions with 4,096 rollouts and a perplexity comparison.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: The main conclusion does not claim this as a general result.

limitations.name: Binary-reward scope
limitations.description: The main framework currently assumes binary reward and does not directly extend to continuous/arbitrary rewards.

limitations.name: Zero-success gradient starvation
limitations.description: If no sampled rollout succeeds, the practical estimators give zero gradient for that task.

limitations.name: Finite rollout approximation
limitations.description: Finite T approximates rather than equals the infinite ML expansion; practical baseline shifts unbiased truncation from N to N−1.

limitations.name: On-policy scope
limitations.description: Experiments intentionally use fully on-policy updates and leave off-policy PPO-style training for future work.

limitations.name: Baseline guarantee
limitations.description: The average-score baseline is empirically helpful but lacks a theoretical variance-reduction guarantee.

limitations.name: Perfect-verifier condition on efficiency
limitations.description: Reported test-time scaling efficiency explicitly filters solutions with a perfect verifier.

limitations.name: Non-binary evidence scope
limitations.description: The non-binary extension has one initial modified-maze study; full theory and broader evaluation are future work.

statistics_analysis.aggregation_units: ImageNet averages analytic per-image pass@k; non-differentiable pass@k uses task-level correct-count sampling; Table 10 is 30 AIME questions × 4,096 rollouts; Figure 28 uses minibatch gradients.
statistics_analysis.central_and_dispersion: Primary tables/curves show point estimates. Figure 28 uses trace sample covariance, and Figure 29 normalizes by squared expected-gradient norm.
statistics_analysis.uncertainty_reporting: No confidence intervals, p-values, multiple-comparison procedures, or seed-level dispersion are reported in main figures/tables.
statistics_analysis.hierarchy: Observable levels are rollout, prompt/task, dataset/benchmark, gradient minibatch, and model checkpoint; participant level is not applicable.
statistics_analysis.standalone_caption_assessment: Captions generally state task, compared methods, metric, and takeaway, though the non-image Figure 3 caption supplies its lower-is-better convention and training-rollout axis while configuration details remain in Appendix I.
statistics_analysis.significance_vs_mechanism: No formal significance testing is reported; empirical performance, behavioral mechanism evidence, and scope claims should remain distinct.

rhetoric_analysis.strong_vs_weak_claim_pattern: Strong claims occur in abstract/takeaways and are often scope-qualified; mechanism and non-binary claims use suggest/conjecture/future-work language.
rhetoric_analysis.tokenization_risk: pass@k, p_theta, MaxRL, GRPO, RLOO, and hyphenated low-success should not be split into generic word counts.

final_judgment.single_storyline: In terminal binary correctness tasks, MaxRL turns additional rollout compute into a higher-order finite approximation of the maximum-likelihood objective, rather than only a lower-variance estimate of expected reward.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The main body keeps the pass@k expansion, finite T objective, Theorems 1–2 statements, Algorithm 1, weight-function explanation, core ImageNet/maze/GSM8K/Qwen3 results, and concise binary/on-policy boundaries.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: The appendix moves proofs, exact implementation/hyperparameters, pass@k calculation, broader baseline tables, variance/SNR analysis, capability proxy, and a preliminary non-binary extension.
final_judgment.best_pattern: The strongest pattern is theory identity → compact estimator contrast → controlled benchmark with exact ML → progressively realistic scaling results, with one Takeaway box per result block.
final_judgment.largest_gap: The central empirical comparisons do not report random seeds, independent-run dispersion, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests; mechanism evidence is aligned behavior rather than a causal intervention.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: Make the new training objective, the estimator target, and the first controlled empirical consequence refer to the same mathematical quantity before scaling the claim.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This pattern depends on a verifiable event and a tractable population objective; it must be re-derived for continuous rewards, multi-turn trajectories, off-policy learning, or imperfect verifiers.
final_judgment.narrative_structure: scope → objective mismatch → compute-indexed remedy → estimator equivalence → controlled validation → scaling regimes → related-work contrast → concise scope boundary
final_judgment.layout_assessment: Main text uses dense double-column theory/results with cross-column figures and result boxes; appendix switches to single-column proofs and reproducibility detail.

evidence_coverage.coverage_method: Counted every structured substantive evidence record, including page-map, module, claim, visual, theory, design, result, limitation, and appendix evidence.
